1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: Basic information: The patient is a 39-year-old woman who was admitted to the Fifth Department of Respiratory Medicine, The First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University, on Day 0, with the chief complaint of "dyspnea for 2 months, worsened for 16 days." Two months before admission, after COVID-19 infection, the patient developed "dyspnea with chest tightness, worsened after activity, accompanied by fever," with a maximum temperature of 39℃. After self-administered oral antipyretics, her temperature returned to normal; she had no further fever and no discomfort such as cough or sputum production. Sixteen days before admission, she developed dyspnea without obvious precipitating factors, worse than before, accompanied by bilateral lower extremity edema, without fever, cough, sputum production, chest pain, hemoptysis, dizziness, or headache. She presented to a hospital in Runan County, where chest X-ray and chest CT were performed (report unavailable). The outside hospital provided symptomatic supportive treatment (details of diagnosis and treatment unknown). After treatment, her dyspnea improved slightly compared with before. She intermittently used inhaled "budesonide/formoterol" outside the hospital, but the above symptoms still recurred repeatedly. For further diagnosis and treatment, she came to our hospital. Outpatient CTPA showed: 1. suspected small pulmonary emboli in partial branches of the right pulmonary artery; 2. suspected pulmonary hypertension; 3. mildly enlarged cardiac silhouette; 4. suspected varices of the lower thoracic esophagus; 5. cirrhosis; 6. splenomegaly. Echocardiography showed: left atrial enlargement, decreased left ventricular diastolic function, EF 63%; pulmonary artery pressure 28 mmHg. She was admitted from the outpatient clinic with "1. Dyspnea, cause to be determined: pulmonary embolism?; 2. Autoimmune hepatitis; 3. Diabetes mellitus." Since disease onset, the patient has had normal appetite, normal sleep, normal urination and defecation, and no weight loss. Past history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus was diagnosed 8 years ago; during this period she regularly took oral "metformin 0.5 mg, 2 tablets each morning and evening" and reported that blood glucose control was acceptable. Autoimmune hepatitis was diagnosed 6 years ago; she regularly took oral "Ganshuang granules 3 g, 1 sachet three times a day." No history of hypertension or heart disease, no history of cerebrovascular disease, no history of TB or malaria. Vaccination history followed routine social immunization. No history of surgery, trauma, or blood transfusion. No food or drug allergy history. The patient was born in Runan County, Henan Province, and has lived locally for a long time. No history of residence in pastoral areas, mining areas, high-fluoride areas, or iodine-deficient areas. No history of exposure to chemical substances, radioactive substances, or toxic substances. No history of drug abuse. No smoking or alcohol use. Her parents, 1 younger brother, 1 son, 1 daughter, and spouse are healthy. Physical examination: temperature 36.60℃, pulse 86/min, respiratory rate 18/min, blood pressure 125/65 mmHg, SPO2 92% (not on oxygen). General examination: normal development, well-proportioned build, clear consciousness, in fair spirits, no jaundice of the skin or mucous membranes, no subcutaneous edema, no palmar erythema, no spider angiomas. Respiratory movements were normal, intercostal spaces were normal, tactile fremitus was normal, no pleural friction fremitus, no subcutaneous crepitus, percussion was resonant, breath sounds were clear in both lungs, with no dry or moist rales, and no pleural friction rub. No obvious abnormalities were found on abdominal, neurologic, or other examinations. Laboratory tests: Arterial blood gas analysis: pH 7.475↑, PCO2 29.40↓ mmHg, PO2 57.0↓ mmHg, total hemoglobin 106.00↓ g/L, hematocrit 32.40↓%, oxygen saturation 88.40↓%. Complete blood count: white blood cell count 3.42↓×10^9/L, red blood cell count 4.96×10^12/L, hemoglobin 108.0↓ g/L, platelet count 115↓×10^9/L. Coagulation tests: prothrombin time 15.30↑ s, prothrombin activity 62.00↓%, activated partial thromboplastin time 40.30↑ s, D-dimer 0.14 mg/L. Blood biochemistry: ALT 21 U/L, AST 31 U/L, albumin 37.3 g/L, globulin 36.6↑ g/L, direct bilirubin 9.2 μmol/L, indirect bilirubin 14.6↑ μmol/L, creatine kinase-MB 43.8↑ U/L. NT-proBNP 39.2 pg/mL. Hemoglobin A1c: 6.5%. No obvious abnormalities were found in the infectious disease panel of four items, routine urine and stool tests, 3 inflammatory markers, renal function, electrolytes, lipid panel of four items, fasting blood glucose, or thyroid function. Pathogen-related indicators: comprehensive viral panel negative. Immune-related indicators: ANCA 4-item panel + comprehensive connective tissue disease panel: ANA (IgG type): 1:100 (±) (speckled + nucleolar pattern), the rest negative. Autoimmune liver panel: anti-gastric parietal cell antibody positive (1:320). Comprehensive rheumatoid arthritis panel: rheumatoid factor IgM type 32.6 ↑ IU/mL, the rest negative. Antiphospholipid antibody panel: all negative. Immunoglobulins and complement: IgG 18.32 ↑ g/L, IgE 217 ↑ IU/mL, complement C3 0.83↓ g/L. On Day -2, the patient underwent CTPA + chest CT at our hospital. CTPA showed indistinct low-density filling defects in the branch arteries of the anterior segment of the right upper lobe (im229) and the posterior basal segment of the right lower lobe; low-density shadow was seen in local branches of the medial segment of the right middle lobe. The main pulmonary artery was mildly dilated, with a diameter of about 35 mm; the remaining main left and right pulmonary arteries and branches were well visualized, with no luminal stenosis or dilation and no filling defects in the lumen. The examination showed acceptable translucency of both lungs, clear markings, and no abnormal density shadows in either lung. Bilateral hilar shadows were not enlarged. The trachea and bronchi were patent. The bilateral thoraces were symmetric. No enlarged lymph nodes were seen in the mediastinum or axillae. The cardiac silhouette was mildly enlarged. No pleural effusion or pleural thickening was seen bilaterally. The visualized wall of the lower thoracic esophagus was irregularly thickened; the visualized liver margin was slightly irregular, the spleen was enlarged, and multiple collateral vessels were seen around it. Diagnostic impression: suspected small pulmonary emboli in partial branches of the right pulmonary artery; suspected pulmonary hypertension. Mildly enlarged cardiac silhouette. Suspected varices of the lower thoracic esophagus. Visualized cirrhosis and splenomegaly. Ultrasonography findings: heart—left atrial enlargement, decreased left ventricular diastolic function; liver/gallbladder/spleen/pancreas—enlarged liver with diffuse parenchymal echogenic changes, thickened gallbladder wall; thyroid and cervical lymph nodes—bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy; urinary system—no obvious abnormality; lower extremity veins—valvular insufficiency of the deep veins of both lower extremities.

differential_diagnoses.name: Acute or subacute pulmonary embolism
supporting_evidence: Chief complaint: “dyspnea for 2 months, worsening for 16 days”; progressive dyspnea present
Arterial blood gas analysis showed PaO2 57.0mmHg↓, oxygen saturation 88.40%↓, and PaCO2 29.40mmHg↓, consistent with hypoxemia with hypocapnia, which can be seen in pulmonary embolism

CTPA showed "ill-defined low-density filling defects in the branch arteries of the anterior segment of the right upper lobe and the posterior basal segment of the right lower lobe; a low-density shadow was visible in some local branches of the medial segment of the right middle lobe"; the diagnostic impression was "small pulmonary emboli in some branches of the right pulmonary artery"
Outpatient CTPA also indicated "consider pulmonary hypertension"

16 days ago, bilateral lower extremity edema developed, and venous Doppler ultrasound of both lower extremities showed "bilateral deep venous valvular insufficiency of the lower extremities," suggesting a background risk for venous thromboembolism
opposing_evidence: No chest pain, hemoptysis, or tachycardia. On physical examination, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, pulse 86 beats/min; vital signs relatively stable.
The pulmonary arteries only suggest a small amount of embolism in some branches; the imaging burden may not fully correlate with the severity of the marked hypoxemia

differential_diagnoses.name: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary vascular disease/chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPD/CTEPH)
supporting_evidence: Dyspnea has persisted for 2 months with recurrent episodes, suggesting that this is not merely a transient acute process.
CTPA showed filling defects in the branches of the pulmonary artery, and also indicated "pulmonary hypertension"
CTPA showed slight dilation of the main pulmonary artery, with a diameter of approximately 35 mm
Hypoxemia present: PaO2 57.0 mmHg↓, oxygen saturation 88.40%↓

Both the imaging and the written report indicate that the pulmonary parenchyma is essentially clear, with no abnormal density opacities seen in either lung, supporting the possibility of a pulmonary vascular lesion.
opposing_evidence: Echocardiography showed pulmonary artery pressure of 28 mmHg, which does not support definite significant pulmonary hypertension.
The disease course is currently only 2 months, and the evidence for typical chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension is still insufficient.
No prior definite history of venous thrombosis or recurrent pulmonary embolism was provided in the first-stage information.

differential_diagnoses.name: Hepatopulmonary syndrome (hypoxemia associated with cirrhosis/portal hypertension)
supporting_evidence: CT and color Doppler ultrasound indicated “cirrhosis, splenomegaly, and multiple collateral vessels visible peripherally,” and lower thoracic esophageal varices were also considered, suggesting a background of portal hypertension.
The patient has a 6-year history of autoimmune hepatitis, with underlying chronic liver disease.
Arterial blood gas analysis showed significant hypoxemia: PaO2 57.0 mmHg↓, oxygen saturation 88.40%↓

Chest CT showed preserved bilateral lung lucency and clear lung markings; no abnormal density shadows were seen in either lung, and the hypoxemia cannot be explained by obvious pulmonary parenchymal lesions.
On physical examination, breath sounds were clear in both lungs, with no dry or moist rales, supporting an extrapulmonary or pulmonary vascular cause of hypoxemia
opposing_evidence: The first-stage information did not provide manifestations more supportive of hepatopulmonary syndrome, such as orthopnea-associated hypoxemia, digital clubbing, and spider angiomas.
CTPA has already identified filling defects in branches of the pulmonary artery, and hypoxemia can also be explained by pulmonary embolism.
In the first stage, no contrast-enhanced ultrasound or direct evidence of intrapulmonary vascular dilatation was provided.

differential_diagnoses.name: Portopulmonary hypertension
supporting_evidence: The patient has evidence of chronic liver disease and portal hypertension: a history of autoimmune hepatitis; CT indicates cirrhosis, splenomegaly, collateral circulation formation, and esophageal varices.
The main symptom is dyspnea, which worsens after exertion, consistent with a common manifestation of pulmonary hypertension.
CTPA indicated "consider pulmonary hypertension," and the main pulmonary artery trunk was mildly dilated to approximately 35 mm
Arterial blood gas analysis showed hypoxemia
opposing_evidence: Echocardiography showed pulmonary artery pressure of 28 mmHg, not supporting definite pulmonary arterial hypertension.
NT-proBNP 39.2 pg/mL, not suggestive of significant increased right heart strain
CTPA has shown filling defects in the branches of the pulmonary arteries, and the dyspnea can initially be explained by pulmonary embolism.

supporting_evidence: Echocardiography showed left atrial enlargement and decreased left ventricular diastolic function, suggesting the presence of left ventricular diastolic dysfunction
CT showed a slightly enlarged cardiac silhouette; the attached image also demonstrates an enlarged cardiac silhouette
Symptoms include chest tightness and dyspnea on exertion; accompanied by bilateral lower extremity edema 16 days earlier, which can be seen in cardiac insufficiency.
opposing_evidence: Left ventricular ejection fraction EF 63%, preserved systolic function
Pro-B-type natriuretic peptide 39.2 pg/mL, not suggestive of significant heart failure
No moist rales on lung examination; CT showed no pulmonary edema or pleural effusion.

recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient presented primarily with dyspnea persisting for 2 months and worsening over the past 16 days, with marked hypoxemia and hypocapnia even at rest (PaO2 57.0mmHg, SaO2 88.40%, PaCO2 29.40mmHg). However, chest CT showed hyperlucent bilateral lungs without obvious parenchymal lesions, and the pulmonary physical examination was also essentially negative, suggesting that the hypoxemia was not concordant with pulmonary parenchymal disease. Although an earlier single-phase CTPA showed a small filling defect in a branch of the pulmonary artery, the D-dimer was not elevated, and the ventilation-perfusion scan showed no typical signs of pulmonary embolism, while also suggesting the presence of a right-to-left shunt. Therefore, further contrast echocardiography of the right heart is needed to determine whether a shunt is present and to clarify the nature of the shunt. The patient also has a background of portal hypertension, including autoimmune hepatitis, cirrhosis, splenomegaly, collateral circulation formation, and esophageal varices, making hepatopulmonary syndrome an important diagnostic consideration. The core purpose of this examination is to confirm or exclude an intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt, distinguish whether the hypoxemia is primarily caused by pulmonary embolism, cardiac factors, or hepatopulmonary syndrome/intrapulmonary vascular dilatation, and provide key evidence for subsequent diagnostic confirmation, further ultrasound interpretation, and selection of treatment strategy.

The patient currently has dyspnea, and imaging shows enlargement of the main pulmonary artery, suggesting pulmonary hypertension; right heart catheterization is needed for further confirmation of whether pulmonary hypertension is present.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: Right heart contrast echocardiography was completed. According to the ultrasound findings, after injection of the right heart contrast agent through the median cubital vein, dense contrast echoes were seen in the right atrium and right ventricle; after five cardiac cycles, a large amount of contrast echoes was seen in the left heart, with slow clearance. Ultrasound impression: right heart contrast echocardiography—positive right heart contrast study (+RLS grade: III) (consider pulmonary arteriovenous fistula or arteriovenous malformation).

8.final_diagnosis_and_diagnostic_basis.final_diagnosis: Hepatopulmonary syndrome, Type I respiratory failure, cirrhosis, splenomegaly, esophagogastric varices, decreased white blood cell count, hemoglobin, and platelet count
diagnostic_basis: The patient is a young woman with a 6-year history of autoimmune liver disease.
Arterial blood gas indicated type I respiratory failure; white blood cell count, hemoglobin, and platelet count were decreased; D-dimer was not elevated; indirect bilirubin was elevated

The patient was previously seen in the relevant department of our hospital in approximately 92 months before Day 0 and approximately 62 months before Day 0 for "cirrhosis." Based on the current test results and the patient's imaging findings, cirrhosis, splenomegaly, and esophagogastric varices are indicated.

Right heart contrast echocardiography - right heart contrast study (+RLS grade: III): after five cardiac cycles, a large amount of contrast agent echo is visible in the left heart, with slow clearance (consider pulmonary arteriovenous fistula or arteriovenous malformation)

Lung ventilation-perfusion results showed: fused pulmonary perfusion tomographic imaging revealed no typical signs of pulmonary embolism; both kidneys were visualized, suggesting the presence of a right-to-left shunt; a small amount of fibrotic streaking in the left lung. Pulmonary artery thromboembolism was excluded.
